Article Title: Sharad Pawar’s MPs to meet PM Modi; Congress asks them to delink women’s quota, delimitation
Article Text:
NCP(SP) to meet PM Modi, delegation to raise issues affecting Maharashtra,.

NCP (SP) MPs to raise Maharashtra issues

NEW DELHI: A delegation of eight MPs from Sharad Pawar-led NCP (SP) is scheduled to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday during the ongoing Monsoon Session of Parliament.Ahead of the meeting, the Congress has urged its alliance partner to convey the INDIA bloc's opposition to linking the implementation of women's reservation with the proposed delimitation exercise.AICC secretary Sachin Sawant urged the NCP (SP) delegation to press Modi for the immediate implementation of the Women's Reservation Act, passed in 2023, without waiting for delimitation."It is learnt that the MPs of the Nationalist Congress Party - Sharadchandra Pawar will be meeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday regarding issues concerning Maharashtra. We urge them to firmly convey to Prime Minister Modi that the INDIA Alliance's unequivocal position is that the Women's Reservation Act, passed in 2023, must be implemented immediately and should not be linked to delimitation," Sawant posted on X on Sunday."It is important that the unity of the INDIA Alliance and its opposition to the Modi government on this issue is made unequivocally clear," he added.The Congress' appeal comes ahead of the meeting between PM Modi and eight NCP (SP) MPs, led by party MP Supriya Sule.Sule had said on Saturday that the delegation would raise issues affecting Maharashtra, including farmer suicides, the water crisis and problems caused by rapid urbanisation."We - some MPs and I - were talking about that Prime Minister must be apprised about the problems in Maharashtra. There is water related issues, farmer suicides, and problems being faced due to urbanisation," Sule said at a press conference in Mumbai.BJP leader Navneet Rana welcomed the proposed meeting, saying elected representatives should be able to raise issues concerning Maharashtra's development with the Prime Minister."I feel that if MPs from Sharad Pawar 's party are meeting PM Modi for the sake of Maharashtra's development--driven by the belief that the state needs to progress further--then such a meeting is certainly not a bad thing," Rana said."While all sorts of speculations are being made, I believe any such speculation ultimately bodes well for Maharashtra; there could be nothing better than them approaching the PM to advocate for the state's development," she added.The dispute centres on the government's proposed delimitation exercise and its connection with the implementation of the women's reservation law. The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, introduced in the Lok Sabha on April 16, proposed increasing the strength of the House to 850 seats and sought to expedite the implementation of the Women's Reservation Act passed in 2023.The bill, however, failed to secure the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of members present and voting and was not passed during the extended Budget Session.The Congress and other opposition parties have backed women's reservation but oppose making its implementation dependent on delimitation. They have argued that the reservation provisions should be implemented immediately rather than waiting for the expansion and redrawing of Lok Sabha constituencies.
Article Summary: NCP (SP) MPs to meet PM Modi, delegation to raise issues affecting Maharashtra. Congress has urged its alliance partner to convey the INDIA bloc's opposition to linking the implementation of women's reservation with the proposed delimitation exercise. AICC secretary Sachin Sawant urged the NCP delegation to press Modi for the immediate implementation of the Women's Reservation Act, passed in 2023.

Article Title: To bypass Bosphorus & Hormuz, Russia moots direct rail link to India
Article Text:
Apart from logistical difficulty and cost, for any option to extend the rail link to India, New Delhi would have to deal with the fact that it would pass through Pakistan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Russian deputy PM Marat Khusnullin has suggested exploring a direct rail link from Moscow to the ‘Indian Ocean’ to avert risks associated with the Bosphorus and the Strait of Hormuz, amid ongoing conflicts, including in West Asia, that have stalled the ambitious India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor. Bosphorus is a narrow, natural strait in Turkey that connects Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara.“A rail link to the Indian Ocean should also be explored. Risks related to the Bosphorus and the Strait of Hormuz might require alternative routes: through Turkmenistan, Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. Any options providing access to India are acceptable,” he told Russian news agency TASS.Experts said constructing a rail link spanning two continents and four countries would be a gigantic challenge. Apart from logistical difficulty and cost, for any option to extend the rail link to India, New Delhi would have to deal with the fact that it would pass through Pakistan, and a lot would depend on obtaining an iron-clad guarantee for securing cooperation and commitment of the hostile neighbour to protect the railway and cargo.The statement does not provide a detailed construction plan, cost estimate or timeline. However, if such a corridor is eventually developed, it could create a direct overland rail freight route linking Russia with India while offering an alternative to traditional maritime shipping routes.Among railway corridors linking multiple nations, Yiwu-Madrid is the longest freight train line in the world — spanning a little over 13,000 km, it connects China’s Yiwu to Spain’s Madrid, traversing eight countries.
Article Summary: Russian deputy PM Marat Khusnullin has suggested exploring a direct rail link from Moscow to the ‘Indian Ocean’ This would avert risks associated with the Bosphorus and the Strait of Hormuz, amid ongoing conflicts, including in West Asia.

Article Title: Dope test of turbulent Air India flight’s pilot ‘not negative’, sent for confirmation, says government

NEW DELHI: The captain of Air India’s August 4 Phuket-Delhi flight, which experienced a sudden loss of altitude of about 300 feet, was subjected to a psychoactive substance (dope) screening test on arrival, whose result was “not negative” and has been sent for confirmatory tests, the aviation ministry said Sunday.TOI had exclusively reported on Sunday that the pilot of the turbulence-hit flight may have failed the dope test.The ministry has classified the incident, which led to 17 people being hospitalised, as serious and said the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) will probe it.“Further action, as appropriate, will be taken based on the outcome of the investigation and confirmatory test results,” it said.Directorate General of Civil Aviation rules stipulate that “in case the screening test (for psychoactive substances) is non-negative, the employee shall be immediately removed from the safety-sensitive duty till a confirmatory report is received. In case of positive confirmatory test for the first time, the concerned employee shall be referred by the organisation” for de-addiction.Multiple passengers and cabin crew members on board the Airbus A320 operating as AI 2379 were injured when it suddenly lost altitude. The plane later landed safely in Delhi. “As standard operating procedures following such an occurrence, both flight crew members underwent the prescribed psychoactive substance screening test. The screening test in respect of the pilot-in-command (PIC) indicated a result requiring confirmatory testing. Samples have been sent to the designated laboratory for confirmatory analysis, and the final report is awaited,” the ministry statement added.Both pilots have been taken off flying duty by the DGCA, pending investigation.
Article Summary: The captain of Air India’s August 4 Phuket-Delhi flight was subjected to a psychoactive substance (dope) screening test on arrival. The result was “not negative” and has been sent for confirmatory tests. ToI had exclusively reported on Sunday that the pilot of the turbulence-hit flight may have failed the dope test.

Article Title: Captain of turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight may have failed dope test
Article Text:
The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet.

NEW DELHI: The captain operating Air India’s turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight on Tuesday (Aug 4) reportedly tested positive in a psychoactive substances (dope) test conducted on arrival, according to multiple sources. The airline did not either confirm or deny it, saying while the tests were conducted, the results have not been shared with it.“We are aware that a post-flight screening test was conducted on the pilots in accordance with applicable protocols. However, the results of the test have not been shared with Air India, and we are therefore not in a position to comment on any findings,” an AI spokesperson said.“Air India undertakes regular drug testing of crew members in compliance with civil aviation regulations, independent of any specific flight or operational incident. We will continue to cooperate with the relevant authorities as required,” the airline added.The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet. On arrival in Delhi, 13 passengers and four crew members were hospitalised. Sources say the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is probing this case from all angles including whether the handling of this turbulence event was correct; whether the event happened due to weather or some other reason; the likely impact on the aircraft like did it suffer hydraulic failure due to impact and whether it should have flown all the way to Delhi after the episode and not diverted to some nearby airport like Varanasi or Lucknow.Pending probe, flight crew is taken off flying duty as per protocol. So the pilots of this flight are also not flying currently. DGCA rules stipulate that a pilot testing positive for consumption of psychoactive substances for the first time be referred to for de-addiction and rehabilitation. Such crew member can return for active duties with a negative dope test report.But after resuming flying if the same person tests positive for psychoactive substances again, their licence will be suspended for three years. And if after resuming flying the same person again tests positive for the third time, the flying licence is cancelled.International Civil Aviation Organisation says that “holders of licences shall not exercise the privileges of their licences and related ratings while under the influence of any psychoactive substance, which might render them unable to safely and properly exercise these privileges”.While the probe in Tuesday’s event would have focused on pilot handling the situation anyway, the captain reportedly testing positive adds another dimension to the same.
Article Summary: The captain operating Air India’s turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight reportedly tested positive in a psychoactive substances (dope) test. The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet. 13 passengers and four crew members were hospitalised.

NEW DELHI: On July 1, an attack by pirates on an India-bound bulk carrier, Golden Arsenal, in the Gulf of Aden was foiled after the captain moved all crew members, including an Indian seafarer, into the vessel’s “citadel” and sought assistance from the Indian Navy A citadel is a fortified safe room with essential supplies such as food and water, as well as communication equipment, where crew members can take refuge during a pirate attack. The pirates failed to breach the citadel and eventually fled the vessel.Sharing this incident at the National Port Security Conference this week, Captain Vikram Singh Manhas, deputy nautical adviser at DGMA (maritime regulator), urged all crew members and masters to remain vigilant and follow preventive measures prescribed under best management practices (BMP), amid a rise in piracy incidents.Four vessels are held hostage by Somali pirates at present, three of which have Indian crew members aboard.One of the vessels has one Indian seafarer, while the other two have five and 11 Indian crew, respectively.Highlighting the significance of prevention in such cases, Manhas said that once a vessel is held by pirates, everything is dependent upon the negotiations with the pirates and that the government is working to ensure the safe release of Indian seafarers.In the direction of ensuring their safety, the government is set to launch a dashboard on August 15 to track every Indian seafarer on any ship. Additionally, shipping and ports minister Sarbananda Sonowal Saturday launched e-Samudra, a digital platform integrating services for seafarers, shipping companies, ports and other maritime stakeholders, and said, “Every Indian seafarer must be safe, respected and supported as India strengthens its position as a global maritime power. ”

NEW DELHI: In a fresh crackdown on food safety violations, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has acted against two food products, penalising the manufacturer of a fortified sunflower oil after it was found to be substandard and stopping the sale of a Monk Fruit Sweetener over alleged licensing and labelling violations.The regulator imposed a penalty on AWL Agri Business Ltd, Mangaluru, after a laboratory analysis of a retail sample of Fortune "Fryola" Refined Sunflower Seed Oil found that its vitamin D content was below the prescribed standard, making the fortified edible oil substandard under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.FSSAI said the company was given an opportunity to present its case, but the adjudicating authority concluded that it had manufactured and marketed a substandard fortified edible oil before imposing a monetary penalty.In a separate action, the regulator prohibited the sale of PIE Foods' Monk Fruit Sweetener, a natural zero-calorie sugar substitute, after inspections found cartons of the product stored at the company's premises without the required manufacturing licence.FSSAI also alleged that the product carried claims such as "100% Monk Fruit Extract" and "Natural Ingredients", while its online listing did not carry the mandatory endorsement required under food safety regulations.It further said the company failed to produce records showing that the monk fruit extract used in the product had been procured in accordance with the Food Safety and Standards Act.The prohibition order will remain in force until the product complies with the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act and related regulations.The regulator said the actions are part of its ongoing drive to tighten enforcement against food business operators and ensure that products sold to consumers meet prescribed safety and quality standards.
Article Summary: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has acted against two food products. The regulator penalised the manufacturer of a fortified sunflower oil after it was found to be substandard. NEW DELHI: ED filed two chargesheets, one each against Reliance Communications (RCom) and Reliance Infrastructure Ltd, on Saturday before a special court here, naming Gautam Doshi, Sateesh Seth, Amitabh Jhunjhunwala and the two entities of Anil Ambani's Reliance Group as the accused for offences of money laundering and defalcation of bank funds of over Rs 40,000 crore.In its chargesheet against RCom, the agency has said that "the proceeds of crime are quantified at Rs 40,186 crore, the outstanding sum defaulted on by the entities to a consortium of banks and financial institutions".The role of the accused in the raising, deployment, concealment and projection of the funds, including false certification of end-use of $1 billion in FCCB proceeds, was also highlighted.ED sought confiscation of properties worth Rs 8,078 crore attached earlier in the case, belonging to Reliance Communications and its promoters and directors, including assets of Anil Ambani.The chargesheet against Reliance Infrastructure Ltd said, "Probe revealed an organised scheme to divert public funds from four NHAI-awarded toll-road projects: Trichy-Karur (NH-67), Trichy-Dindigul (NH-45), Salem-Ulundurpet (NH-68) and Jaipur-Reengus (NH-11). Regarding RCom, it said, "Fresh credit facilities were fraudulently used to repay, rotate domestic...liabilities instead of the sanctioned end-use."

Article Title: Recent rain has little impact on national monsoon deficit
Article Text:
IMD, however, predicted a rise in rainfall activity over Bengal, Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Bihar from Aug 13 onwards

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Good rains in the past one week over Delhi, Haryana and east Rajasthan helped offset the shortfall in these areas, but they did not reduce the overall country-wide monsoon deficit by much. In this period, India's cumulative rainfall deficit was down by only one percentage point - from 12% on Aug 2 to 11% on Aug 9 - with many agrarian states, including Bihar, Jharkhand, UP, Punjab and Andhra Pradesh, continuing to witness deficient rainfall.It rained in many parts at a time when sowing of Kharif crops had ended in almost 88% of the country's total sown area. As a result, the acreage deficit could be reduced by only 1% in the past one week, with paddy, the main kharif crop, still reporting 4% less acreage compared to the corresponding period last year. Aug rains will improve water storage in reservoirs, which is a good augury for hydro-power potential being utilised and a back-up being in place for the next sowing season. As of Sunday, as many as 12 states have reported high rain deficits of 20% and more.IMD on Sunday, however, predicted a rise in rainfall activity over Bengal, Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Bihar from Aug 13 onwards due to possible formation of a low-pressure area over the north Bay of Bengal and Bengal-Bangladesh coasts around Thursday. This may, to some extent, revive sowing of paddy and maize in Bihar and Jharkhand. Region-wise, all regions, except central India, have reported cumulative monsoon rainfall deficit despite 'normal' rains in July and in the first week of August, with east and northeast India recording the highest deficit of 25%, followed by 17% in south peninsular India and 11% in northwest India.
Article Summary: India's cumulative rainfall deficit was down by only one percentage point. Many agrarian states, including Bihar, Jharkhand, UP, Punjab and Andhra Pradesh, continue to witness deficient rainfall. As many as 12 states have reported high rain deficits of 20% and more.

Article Title: India, Russia to be linked by rail? Moscow floats proposal, calls it 'viable'
Article Text:
Russian deputy PM Marat Khusnullin made the suggestion

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin has called on Moscow and New Delhi to explore the feasibility of a direct rail link to the Indian Ocean, aimed at reducing transit risks associated with the Bosphorus strait and Strait of Hormuz.According to Khusnullin, potential routes could pass through Turkmenistan, Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan, adding that any corridor providing connectivity to India would be considered “viable.”If realised, the proposal would create a direct overland rail freight link between Russia and India.“A rail link to the Indian Ocean should also be explored. Risks related to the Bosphorus and the Strait of Hormuz might require alternative routes: through Turkmenistan, Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. Any options providing access to India are acceptable,” Khusnullin was quoted as saying by TASS.The proposal comes amid disruptions to maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz following the escalation of hostilities between the US-Israel and Iran. On February 28, the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran, targeting key urban centres, including Tehran. Iran responded with missile and drone attacks on Israeli targets and US military bases across Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE and Saudi Arabia.Tehran subsequently announced a maritime blockade of the Strait of Hormuz targeting vessels linked to the US, Israel and allied countries involved in the conflict. The strategic waterway handles around 20% of global oil trade and nearly 20% of worldwide LNG shipments.Meanwhile, Türkiye briefly restricted access to the Bosphorus strait following attacks on vessels in the strait, including Turkish-owned ships.Beyond international transport links, Khusnullin also highlighted the need for sustained investment in Russia’s construction sector. He said the industry currently has the capacity to absorb an additional one trillion rubles annually.“The construction industry is already capable of handling an additional one trillion rubles annually. However, if such a volume is secured for the next five years, it would be possible to expand capacity and build even more,” he added.
Article Summary: Russian Deputy PM Marat Khusnullin has called on Moscow and New Delhi to explore the feasibility of a direct rail link to the Indian Ocean. The proposal comes amid disruptions to maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz following the escalation of hostilities between the US and Iran.

Article Title: ED director Rahul Navin's tenure extended by a year
Article Text:
After three years as ED director, Navin could get two more extensions and serve till Aug 2029, all through PM Modi’s tenure

NEW DELHI: Rahul Navin has been granted a one-year extension as ED director as his two-year fixed tenure was due to end this month.The tenure of Navin, a 1993-batch Indian Revenue Service (I-T) officer, as director of enforcement has been extended for a period of one year beyond "13.08.2026 i.e. up to 13.08.2027, including extension in service beyond the date of his superannuation or until further orders," as per DoPT.After three years as ED director, he could get two more extensions and serve till August 2029, all through the PM Modi government's tenure, with polls due in April-May 2029.Navin's tenure as director (in-charge) began on September 15, 2023, and he was appointed as ED director on August 14, 2024, while his service retirement was due on July 31, 2027. He has set a roadmap for officers to complete probes within two years and ensure attached properties are auctioned and restituted to rightful claimants and fraud victims, including banks or individuals.
Article Summary: Rahul Navin has been granted a one-year extension as ED director. His two-year fixed tenure was due to end this month. He could get two more extensions and serve till August 2029, with polls due in April-May 2029.

The Parliament passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026, amid a wider logjam that has repeatedly disrupted the Monsoon Session. The Rajya Sabha cleared the legislation on Tuesday by voice vote days after the Lok Sabha passed it on July 31 amid opposition protests without a debate.Both Houses witnessed repeated adjournments during the session, with several Bills being passed amid disruptions. The Monsoon Session began on July 20 and is scheduled to conclude on August 13.The new legislation focuses on a seemingly routine but important part of government records like registering births and deaths. A birth certificate records a person's entry into the official system, while a death certificate formally records their departure.Together, these documents help establish identity, maintain public records and provide proof for a range of legal and administrative purposes. The amendment seeks to tighten the process when such events are reported long after they occur.Under the existing system, delayed registration already requires additional verification. If information about a birth or death is submitted after one year but within two years, the amended law will require an order from a district magistrate, sub-divisional magistrate or an executive magistrate authorised by the district magistrate.For cases reported more than two years after the event, the threshold becomes higher. The registration will require an order from a judicial magistrate of the First Class having jurisdiction over the place where the birth or death occurred.The magistrate will have to verify the correctness of the information before permitting registration. A prescribed fee will also have to be paid, according to a document released by the government.The amendment also updates the reference to an "Executive Magistrate" in the 1969 law to align it with the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the earlier Code of Criminal Procedure.The government says the primary objective is to ensure that births and deaths are registered promptly and that delayed registrations are subjected to stronger scrutiny.The Registration of Births and Deaths Act makes registration mandatory. According to the government's statement of objects and reasons, birth and death certificates provide legal identity and can be used as evidence of a person's birth or death.The government argues that the integrity of these records is particularly important because birth certificates can be used for several official purposes, including processes involving identity and citizenship-related documentation.Tighter scrutiny of delayed registrations, it says, can help prevent fraudulent or questionable entries and improve the reliability of official records.BJP IT cell head Amit Malviya said, “The objective is straightforward: encourage timely registration, prevent fraudulent or dubious entries, and preserve the credibility of birth and death certificates, the foundational documents that establish a person’s legal identity.”The government has also pointed to a significant rise in registration rates over the past decade.Union minister of state for home Nityanand Rai said birth registration increased from 86.6% in 2014 to 99.1% in 2024, while death registration rose from 72.5% to 99.4% during the same period. He also said around 3.5 lakh registration centres have been established across the country.The government's argument is that as registration coverage approaches universal levels, the focus must increasingly be on ensuring that the remaining delayed or questionable cases are properly verified.A birth certificate is often the first formal document linking an individual to the state. It records details such as a person's date and place of birth and can be required for a range of official purposes, including education, employment, passports and other government documentation.The government has also highlighted the role of birth records in establishing identity and in processes where proof of birth or citizenship-related documentation is required.That makes the accuracy of the registration system important beyond population statistics.A fraudulent birth certificate, for instance, could potentially affect records across several government systems. Similarly, failure to register deaths can leave outdated information in official databases.The government has also linked accurate death registration with keeping records, including electoral rolls, updated.The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on July 31 by voice vote amid opposition protests. Several opposition MPs entered the Well of the House demanding the presence of Union home minister Amit Shah , and the legislation was cleared without a debate.Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju criticised the opposition for not participating in the proceedings and said the government wanted a discussion on the "important Bill".“It is unfortunate. Please do not repeat this in the future. People who sent you to Parliament will seek answers from you,” Rijiju said, urging MPs to participate in debates rather than disrupt proceedings.The legislation was passed amid continued sloganeering, with the opposition MPs demanding the presence of Union home minister Amit Shah and his response on the "police action" against student protesters on July 20 at Jantar Mantar.The Rajya Sabha later took up the Bill amid similar disruptions.Moving the Bill in the Rajya Sabha, Rai said the government wanted every birth and death to be properly recorded. He said, “The country wants that anyone born in the country, it is important that he or she is registered. Anyone who has died, cannot continue to remain in the voter lists to benefit some parties.”Rai also linked the legislation to concerns over people who have died continuing to appear on electoral rolls.He also cited the rise in registration rates as evidence of the government's efforts to improve the system.Some NDA members supported the legislation. YSRCP member M R Reddy, AIADMK's M Thambidurai and BRS member Ravi Chandra Vaddiraju backed the Bill. BJP member Biswajit Sinha, meanwhile, accused the Congress of opposing the legislation because it did not want proper registration of births and deaths.Sinha also referred to the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in West Bengal, claiming that people who had died years earlier remained on voter lists.He alleged that some parties were helping illegal Bangladeshi and Pakistani infiltrators obtain birth registrations and voter identities, and said the proposed changes would help prevent such practices.Leader of opposition Mallikarjun Kharge said, “The prime minister and the home minister should come. we want discussion.”Despite the protests, the Bill was taken up for consideration and passage.Opposition members did not reject the need for accurate birth and death records but questioned the practical implications of requiring a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class to approve registrations delayed by more than two years.UPPL member Pramod Boro said the objective of the Bill was important but questioned whether an administrative responsibility should be shifted to the judiciary.He warned that the provision could add to the workload of courts, increase costs and make registration more difficult for migrants, homeless people, poor families and those living in remote areas.BJD member Santrupt Misra also questioned why registrations are delayed in the first place. He suggested that the government should identify the reasons behind late registration and consider dedicated registration offices, particularly in tribal areas, to improve access.CPI(M) member V Sivadasan supported the need for proper registration but said the government should also focus on the circumstances surrounding deaths, including malnutrition and student deaths.The passage came amid a wider logjam in the Monsoon Session, with repeated adjournments in both Houses and several Bills being cleared amid disruptions.With Parliament having passed the Bill, the legislation will now go through the remaining constitutional process before coming into force. The Bill, therefore, seeks to strike a balance between two objectives: ensuring that births and deaths are recorded promptly, while subjecting unusually delayed registrations to greater scrutiny.
Article Summary: The Parliament passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026. The Rajya Sabha cleared the legislation on Tuesday by voice vote. The Lok Sabha passed it on July 31 amid opposition protests without a debate. Both Houses witnessed repeated adjournments during the session, with several Bills being passed amid disruptions.

Article Title: What happens after you apply for an organ transplant?
Article Text:
Inside India’s complex journey from transplant registration to surgery

The process starts at the transplant centre

What being on the waiting list actually means

Live Kidneys lead India’s transplant numbers

When a donor organ becomes available

From brain-stem death to retrieval

How India’s transplant numbers have surged

The next stage is a more connected transplant system

For a patient facing end-stage organ failure, being told that a transplant may be required is only the beginning. The journey from a hospital referral to an actual transplant involves medical evaluation, registration, documentation, waitlist management, organ matching, allocation and, eventually, surgery and long-term follow-up.In India, the process is coordinated through a network involving the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation (NOTTO), regional and state-level bodies, registered transplant hospitals and transplant coordinators.The scale of that system has changed sharply. In a February 2026 release, the Press Information Bureau said India recorded nearly 20,000 organ transplants in 2025, compared with fewer than 5,000 in 2013. More than 1,200 families donated the organs of loved ones after death in 2025, the release said.Yet the numbers tell only part of the story. Behind every transplant is a sequence that begins long before the surgeon enters the operating theatre — and, for the recipient, often long before an organ is ever offered. Notto’s says patients are evaluated by a multidisciplinary team, registered through a transplant centre, verified by the relevant allocation body and, once cleared, placed on the appropriate waiting list.A patient with advanced organ failure is first referred to a licensed transplant centre. Doctors assess the underlying disease, the extent of organ damage and whether transplantation is medically appropriate.Not every patient with end-stage organ failure will necessarily be fit for transplantation.Talking about the initial evaluation before transplantation, Dr Manoj Gupta, senior director and HOD, liver transplant, Yatharth Super Speciality Hospital, said, “It typically includes a review of the patient’s medical history, physical examination, blood and tissue tests, imaging, assessment of organ function, infection screening and evaluation of any underlying conditions. Eligibility is determined by several factors, including the patient’s overall health, the extent of organ failure, surgical suitability, the likelihood of benefiting from transplantation and the ability to adhere to the post-transplant treatment regimen. ”However, other factors can also determine eligibility. Dr Goutham Kumar, consultant, HPB & liver transplant services, SPARSH Hospital, added that eligibility also depends on the “absence of absolute contraindications, including active systemic infections, untreated malignancies, severe substance abuse or irreversible co-morbidities.”The hospital and transplant coordinator then compile the information required for registration.Once the application is accepted, the patient's details enter the relevant transplant registry and waiting list. The waiting period can range from the same day to several years.Being on a transplant waiting list is not simply being in a queue. Notto says patients are listed according to medical criteria, with regular and urgent categories, while priority varies by organ. For kidney transplants, time on regular dialysis is among the factors considered; other organs follow different criteria.Dr Kumar explains how these organ-specific criteria work in practice, “Liver allocation often uses the MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) score, while heart allocations prioritize patients on mechanical support. Pediatric patients and high-urgency acute cases frequently receive priority.”Notto’s manual also provides for urgent or “Priority One” categories for patients meeting organ-specific requirements. Such cases may be reviewed by an expert committee before priority is granted, with hospitals required to provide regular clinical updates.Registration does not freeze a patient’s status. Their medical condition continues to be monitored and records updated. Depending on their health, a patient may remain active, be made inactive or become medically unfit for transplantation.The next turn in the journey comes when an organ becomes available. It may come from a living donor, commonly a kidney or part of a liver, or from a deceased donor after certified brain-stem death. At that point, Organ India says, “the transplant coordinator of the hospital will counsel the family and give them the option of donating organs and tissues.”The next of kin must consent before retrieval. That makes a donor pledge only at the beginning of the conversation. Organ India puts it plainly: “In India it's more important to talk to your family about your decision than it is to pledge your organs and get a donor card.”Once a donor organ is identified, a rapid, highly coordinated race against time begins. Blood group compatibility and cross-matching are verified between the donor and potential recipient, while the organ is assessed for suitability.Dr Kumar explains, “A surgical retrieval team harvests the organ and preservation solution is administered. Transport logistics—often utilising dedicated ‘green corridors’ or air transport—are activated to move the organ immediately.”The recipient is called to the hospital, re-evaluated and prepared for surgery, with the surgical team ready to proceed as soon as the donor organ arrives.A deceased donor is medically maintained while permissions and retrieval arrangements are completed, helping preserve viable organs until they can be recovered. Once retrieved, however, the clock begins to run: each organ has a limited preservation window.Cost remains another major barrier to transplantation in India. Dr Kumar said the “initial surgical costs range from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 35 lakh depending on the organ (kidney vs. liver/heart) and hospital sector (public vs. private).” But the financial burden does not end with the operation. Lifelong immunosuppressants, anti-rejection treatment and “regular diagnostic monitoring add Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000 monthly. ”That narrow window makes allocation a tightly coordinated process. Organs are assessed, potential recipients identified and transport arranged.The national system has expanded significantly over the past decade.The ministry said more than 1,200 families came forward to donate the organs of loved ones after death in 2025."More than 4.8 lakh citizens have registered to donate organs and tissues after death through a Aadhaar based verification system, since 17th September 2023," the PIB release said.The release also said India had developed expertise in complex heart, lung and pancreas transplants and claimed the country "leads the world in hands transplants and performs a greater number of hand transplants than any other country."The government said the increase reflected improvements in deceased donation, transplant coordination and national organ sharing.Even after surgery, the process continues. Recipients need lifelong follow-up and immunosuppressive medication, which can also carry long-term risks.Dr Jagriti Yadav, medical director – lab operations, Cryoviva Life Sciences, said, “The major long-term risks include acute or chronic graft rejection, opportunistic infections, cardiovascular complications, kidney toxicity, and metabolic side effects related to immunosuppressive medicines.”The increase in transplant numbers has not eliminated the shortage of organs.A 2024 article published in the National Library of Medicine's PubMed Central noted that India was performing around 17,000-18,000 solid organ transplants a year, making it the world's third-largest transplant country by volume after the United States and China, while transplant rates per million population remained lower than in several high-income countries.Organ India's data and awareness material has similarly highlighted the disparity between the number of patients requiring organs and the number of deceased donors available. The organisation has estimated that India has a large pool of potential brain-stem-death donors but a much smaller number of actual deceased donors.For a patient on a waiting list, that gap translates into uncertainty: being medically eligible and registered does not guarantee that a suitable organ will become available in time.Delhi remains one of the country's major transplant centres.The Delhi government's organ-donation portal provides information on registered hospitals and transplant services and operates under the Health & Family Welfare Department and the State Appropriate Authority. The department's published information lists registered facilities for kidney, liver, heart, lung and pancreas transplantation, as well as eye and cornea services.India’s transplant system also treats foreign nationals, subject to additional safeguards. Government guidance says an Indian living donor may donate to a foreign recipient only if they are near relatives; donors must be at least 18, with medical-visa and registration requirements applicable to both parties.In 2023, India recorded 18,378 transplants and 18,336 individual recipients, including 1,851 foreign nationals, according to Notto data reported in 2024. Delhi recorded the highest number involving foreign recipients at 1,445, followed by Rajasthan at 116 and West Bengal at 88. Only nine involved unrelated deceased-donor organs.For a transplant recipient, perhaps the least visible part of the process is the period between registration and an organ offer.During this period, the patient's condition can change. Tests may have to be repeated, treatment may need adjustment and the transplant centre may update the patient's status on the registry.The patient therefore remains under the care of the transplant team while the allocation system searches for a medically suitable organ.Notto says special requests do not guarantee an immediate organ or override the established rules for matching and allocation.India’s transplant system is becoming more digitally connected, with national coordination and data-sharing expanding alongside transplant numbers. Aadhaar-verified donation registrations crossed 4.8 lakh, while nearly 20,000 transplants were recorded in 2025.The next challenge is ensuring potential donors are identified, families counselled and organs retrieved, transported and allocated efficiently. For recipients, that means staying medically fit, updating the transplant centre and following clinical advice.
Article Summary: India recorded nearly 20,000 organ transplants in 2025, compared with fewer than 5,000 in 2013. Behind every transplant is a sequence that begins long before the surgeon enters the operating theatre. Patients are evaluated by a multidisciplinary team, registered through a transplant centre, verified by the relevant allocation body and placed on the appropriate waiting list.

NEW DELHI: At a time when seven of the country's 25 high courts are without regular chief justices, the Supreme Court collegium, headed by CJI Surya Kant, recommended the names of four HC judges to the government for their appointment as CJs of the Bombay, Calcutta, Patna, and Punjab and Haryana HCs.The collegium recommended appointment of Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi, a judge of Allahabad HC, as CJ of Bombay HC; Justice Ravindra V Ghuge, acting CJ of Bombay HC, as CJ of Calcutta HC; Justice V Kameshwar Rao, a judge of Delhi HC, as CJ of Patna HC; and acting CJ Punjab and Haryana HC Justice Ashwini Kumar Mishra - whose parent high court is Allahabad HC - as regular CJ of that HC.The collegium is yet to decide on selecting judges for appointment as regular CJs to HCs of Rajasthan, J&K and Madhya Pradesh, which are manned by acting CJs - Justices Sanjeev Prakash Sharma, Sanjeev Kumar and Vivek Rusia, respectively.The five-member collegium comprising CJI Kant and Justices Vikram Nath, BV Nagarathna, MM Sundresh and PS Narasimha met separately to recommend the government the transfer of Orissa HC judges Justices Manas Ranjan Pathan and Krushna Ram Mohapatra to Gujarat and Chhattisgarh high courts, respectively, for better administration of justice.Orissa HC has a sanctioned strength of 33 judges but at present it has 17 judges, including the CJ.When these two transfers take effect, the working strength will go down to 15, creating a vacancy of more than 50% of the posts of judges in the HC.Orissa HC Collegium had suggested eight names - four advocates and four judicial officers - for the consideration and scrutiny by SC Collegium and consequent recommendations for appointment as judges of the HC.Since the retirement of CJI Deepak Misra on Oct 2, 2018 - whose tenure towards the end was mired by the controversy of four-most senior SC judges led by Justice J Chelameswar holding an unprecedented presser against the sitting CJI - more than 50 judges have been appointed to SC but Orissa HC has not got representation in the last eight years despite successive CJIs advocating regional and state representation in the top court to make it a truly a national court.
Article Summary: Seven of the country's 25 high courts are without regular chief justices. The Supreme Court collegium recommended the names of four HC judges to the government for their appointment as CJs of the Bombay, Calcutta, Patna, and Punjab and Haryana HCs. The collegium is yet to decide on selecting judges for appointment as regular CJs to HCs of Rajasthan, J&K and Madhya Pradesh.

Article Title: The women who paint Jharkhand: Sohrai-Khovar's journey from ritual to global gallery
Article Text:
Sohrai-Khovar, an ancient women-led art tradition from Jharkhand (Image: TWAC)

What is Sohrai-Khovar?

Ganju Sohrai painted house (Source: TWAC)

Inside of a Khovar room (Source: TWAC)

From mud walls to airport terminals

Painting gifted to Russian President Putin by PM Modi

Tensions surrounding the craft

Gangwa's Lotus - archival art (Source: TWAC)

Pashupati by Kunti Devi (Source: TWAC)

A seat at the table for indigenous art

Exhibition in Rome, 2008 (TWAC)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A local artisan crouches by her doorstep, her hands stained with mud and colour drawn straight from the earth around her. The warmth of rust red, the hush of chalky white, the depth of a black gone nearly charcoal. With nothing more than a broken comb and a steady hand, she draws a peacock on a wall still damp from its coating of clay. In a few hours, this wall, like thousands of others across Hazaribagh, will carry the story of the land of Jharkhand, a mural to its beauty.Sohrai and Khovar paintings are a unique and tribal style of art originating from caves of Jharkhand. In 1991, celebrated and renowned environmentalist Bulu Imam documented rock shelters in the Isco hills of Hazaribagh district and noticed that the motifs on the ancient cave walls closely resembled the paintings still being made on village homes nearbyImam was able to sketch out a connection between the 21st century walls of a home to the Mesolithic and Chalcolithic caves of 10,000 to 5,000 BCE. Other researchers, citing the Archaeological Survey of India, place the rock art closer to 7,000-4,000 BCE, in the Paleolithic period.The dates might be contested but what remains true is that Sohrai and Khovar painting represent one of the longest continuously practiced visual art traditions on the subcontinent, a line running from cave wall to mud wall across several thousand years.Sohrai was originally a season specific craft style painted around the harvest festival of the same name, celebrated after Diwali in the month of Kartik, when households give thanks to their cattle and to the land.Khovar, the word draws from "kho," meaning cave, and "var," meaning groom, is painted for weddings, decorating the room where a newly married couple will spend their first nights together.Both styles of art are made almost exclusively by women. Even its heritage tracing follows matrilineal succession, passed down from mothers to daughters. Traditionally it is classified as a Ma-Beti Parampara, with techniques passed down orally rather than written down.Sanjeev Kumar (IFS), principal chief conservator of forests and head of forest force for Jharkhand, has spent much of his career working alongside these villages. He offers a structural explanation for why this art form became a livelihood tool in the first place, rather than staying purely ceremonial.Jharkhand's rural economy runs largely on two crop cycles a year, he points out, which leaves long stretches when women in farming households have little steady work. Between the sowing and the harvest, there is a kind of enforced pause — and in that pause, an entire category of household income simply goes quiet.Painting, once confined strictly to festival and wedding seasons, has increasingly moved to fill exactly that gap, giving women a way to keep earning in the months the land itself has nothing to offer.It isn't only about income, in Kumar's telling. Starting in 2007, as Divisional Forest Officer in Dhanbad, he began organising folk art camps to give Sohrai a wider audience, drawing participants from across India and as far as Australia and Bangladesh. The camps followed him through later postings — Jamshedpur, Hazaribagh, and beyond — running until the pandemic forced them online, then resuming after. The same women who might once have sat out the off-season are now, through this ecosystem, training relatives, negotiating with buyers, and travelling to exhibitions. Kumar also frames the work as central to the state's eco-tourism ambitions.Sohrai-Khovar finally received Geographical Indication status in May 2020, reportedly approved in under nine months, unusually fast for a process that typically takes two to three years. The tag, granted by the Geographical Indication Registry in Chennai, formally recognises the art as unique to the Hazaribagh region, and gave it a marketing foothold it hadn't had before.The state took the recognition further. Hazaribagh became the first district in Jharkhand to commit to painting all its government buildings with Sohrai motifs — the chief minister's residence, the state secretariat, Ranchi's Birsa Munda Airport, railway stations across Ranchi, Dhanbad, Bokaro, and Tata Nagar all now carry the same red-black-white language once found only on village walls. The art has travelled further still: Prime Minister Modi is reported to have gifted a Sohrai painting to President Putin, a livelihood project turned, however briefly, into an instrument of diplomacy.That visibility has translated into real, traceable livelihoods, in at least some cases. Local organisers connecting artists to buyers report dozens of women directly employed through their networks, hundreds more earning supplemental income in season. Cooperatives built specifically to give village women an alternative to farm labour have carried this work to dozens of international exhibitions across Europe and the US, and increasingly Canada, South Africa, and Japan. Trusts have gone further still — training programmes, small museums, free pigment, and the paperwork that eventually secured the GI tag itself.Not everyone close to this history agrees the shift toward livelihood has been a clean win. Gustav Imam draws a distinction between his father's original vision and the state's current one. Bulu Imam treated Sohrai as fine art from the start — building an exhibition circuit that ran shows in Australia and Europe. The government's livelihood framing, Gustav argues, risks something narrower: pay an artist per piece for a product and you've quietly converted her into daily-wage labour rather than treating her as an artist. He isn't against commercialisation itself; he simply thinks dignity has to come first, and that dignity requires recognition at the very top of the field, not just income at the bottom. Traditions like Madhubani, Warli, and Gond painting have each produced nationally awarded artists, Padma Shri recipients among them; Sohrai-Khovar has not, despite women keeping the tradition alive through real struggle and real limitation. Until a handful of individual artists receive that kind of recognition, he argues, younger painters have no one concrete to aspire to become.He also offers a blunt estimate on the schemes meant to help: of the artisans meant to benefit from government portals and initiatives like Mudra loans, perhaps 5 to 10 percent actually do, largely because many are semi-literate and simply can't navigate the registration process. The rest, in his account, remain outside the system entirely, not excluded by design, but by a bureaucracy that was never built with them in mind.Coal mining is often folded into this story as a single, simple threat, but the picture splits in two once you look closely. The Isco rock art site itself, the discovery that started everything, has not been destroyed. Dust from nearby mines has crept close and settled on it, but the site was declared a national monument around 2023. Other rock art caves in the region, more than a dozen now identified, remain safe largely because, in his words, no one knows about them, obscurity standing in for conservation.The villages are a different story. The North Karanpura coalfield sits beneath a large number of tribal villages across Hazaribagh, Ramgarh, and Chatra, and coal projects in the area have displaced multiple villages over the years, acquiring significant stretches of agricultural land in the process. Residents who've lost land describe rebuilding elsewhere, often some distance from where their families had always lived; local activists warn that further mining could displace still more. Bulu Imam's decades of opposition — intellectual rather than confrontational, built on letters to officials rather than protest, work that earned him the Gandhi International Peace Award in 2012 — was never really about the rock art surviving. It was about whether the people who kept painting around it would get to stay.There is another complication that has nothing to do with mining. Since 2018–19, a central housing scheme, the Pradhan Mantri Gramin Awas Yojana, has replaced mud-and-thatch homes across rural India with brick and cement — a genuine welfare improvement. But Sohrai and Khovar are painted on mud, and the same pigments don't take to cement the same way. One arm of government is quietly removing the canvas that another arm is simultaneously celebrating, not through malice, but through two policies that were never built with each other in mind.The most important complication was hinted at earlier. The market for Sohrai-Khovar remains thin, prices stay low relative to the labour involved, and no fixed floor price exists to stop buyers from talking artists down. Imam suggests that the district administration consider setting a standard pricing for the art to battle some aspects of the issue.The proposed fix, in Gustav's telling, isn't more schemes. It's status. He points to what happens when a piece lands somewhere with real institutional weight — a Sohrai painting, sold to the American ambassador during a visit to Kolkata, now hangs in a prominent hall at the US consulate.Contemporary Indian art by named painters routinely sells for crores; indigenous art too deserves a seat at that table. A tradition this old survives not just on income, but on being taken seriously by the people who could otherwise walk past it without a second look.The artisan finishes her peacock as the light starts to fade. Somewhere else in Hazaribagh, another woman is doing the same. Her red may no longer come from soil gathered by hand, but from a tube of paint bought at the market. The image on the wall is still recognisably Sohrai.For thousands of years, the art has adapted to changing walls, changing materials and changing lives. But preserving it may require more than putting its motifs on government buildings or selling its paintings to new markets. It may mean preserving the women who make it, the homes they paint and the communities that taught them how.The paintings began on cave walls, moved to mud homes and have now travelled to airports, exhibitions and diplomatic gifts. What happens next will depend on whether Sohrai-Khovar is treated simply as a product to be sold — or as a living tradition whose value lies in the people who keep painting it.
Article Summary: Sohrai and Khovar paintings are a unique and tribal style of art originating from caves of Jharkhand. It is one of the longest continuously practiced visual art traditions on the subcontinent. Traditionally it is classified as a Ma-Beti Parampara, with techniques passed down orally rather than written down.

NEW DELHI: The pilots of Air India’s Aug 4 turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight were subjected to psychoactive substance (dope) screening test on arrival at the destination. The pilot-in-command or captain’s screening test report was not negative and has been sent for confirmatory tests, the aviation ministry said on Sunday. The ministry has classified the incident as a serious one which will now be probed by Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB). “Further action, as appropriate, will be taken based on the outcome of the investigation and confirmatory test results,” govt said.Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) rules stipulate that “in case the screening test is non-negative, the employee shall be immediately removed from the safety sensitive duty till a confirmatory report is received. In case of positive confirmatory test for the first time, the concerned employee shall be referred by the organisation” for de-addiction.The aviation ministry on Sunday said: “On Aug 4, Air India A320 (VT-EXO), operating flight AI 2379 from Phuket to Delhi, experienced a sudden loss of altitude of about 300 feet during cruise, following which the aircraft stabilised and subsequently landed safely at Delhi. During the occurrence, injuries were reported to a few passengers and cabin crew members on board.The aircraft was carrying 137 passengers, including three infants, and eight crew members comprising two pilots and six cabin crew. ”“As standard operating procedures following such an occurrence, both flight crew members underwent the prescribed psychoactive substance screening test. The screening test in respect of the pilot-in-command (PIC) indicated a result requiring confirmatory testing. Samples have accordingly been sent to the designated laboratory for confirmatory analysis, and the final report is awaited,” it added.Pending investigation, both pilots have been taken off flying duty by the DGCA. “The aviation ministry and DGCA remain firmly committed to maintaining the highest standards of aviation safety and ensuring that all such occurrences are thoroughly investigated and appropriate action is taken in accordance with the prescribed regulations and procedures,” the statement added.The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet. On arrival in Delhi, 13 passengers and four crew members were hospitalised. People in the know say authorities are probing this case from all angles including whether the handling of this turbulence event was correct; whether the event happened due to weather or some other reason; the likely impact on the aircraft like did it suffer hydraulic failure due to impact and whether it should have flown all the way to Delhi after the episode and not diverted to some nearby airport like Varanasi or Lucknow.DGCA rules stipulate that a pilot testing positive for consumption of psychoactive substances for the first time be referred to for de-addiction and rehabilitation. Such crew member can return for active duties with a negative dope test report.But after resuming flying if the same person tests positive for psychoactive substances again, their licence will be suspended for three years. And if after resuming flying the same person again tests positive for the third time, the flying licence is cancelled.
Article Summary: The pilot-in-command or captain’s screening test report was not negative and has been sent for confirmatory tests. The ministry has classified the incident as a serious one which will now be probed by Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau. Both pilots have been taken off flying duty by the DGCA.

Article Title: AI can help bridge India's healthcare gap: Report
Article Text:
AI is not intended to replace doctors but to multiply specialist capacity by assisting in diagnosis

NEW DELHI: India's healthcare system is coming under growing pressure from an ageing population, rising burden of chronic diseases and shortages of doctors, nurses and hospital beds, according to a knowledge paper released by Union Health Minister J P Nadda on Saturday. The report says artificial intelligence (AI) can help bridge this widening gap by extending specialist expertise, improving diagnosis and expanding access to quality healthcare, particularly in smaller hospitals and underserved areas.Nadda released the knowledge paper, "AI in MedTech: Revolutionizing Healthcare Through Artificial Intelligence," at the 9th edition of India Medical Device 2026, organised by the Department of Pharmaceuticals in association with FICCI.The report estimates India's population at 1.47 billion in 2026 and says more than 65% of deaths are now due to non-communicable diseases such as heart disease, diabetes and cancer. It projects the population aged 60 years and above to cross 230 million by 2036, further increasing demand for long-term healthcare.Despite expansion in healthcare infrastructure and medical education, shortages persist. India has 9.6 doctors per 10,000 population, compared with the global average of 18.3.It has 27.2 nursing personnel per 10,000 against 40.5 globally, 15.9 hospital beds per 10,000 compared with 33, and only 4 MRI scanners per million people, against the global average of 19, the report says.According to the report, AI is not intended to replace doctors but to multiply specialist capacity by assisting in diagnosis, clinical decision-making and screening. AI-enabled diagnostics are expected to be the first large-scale application, helping extend specialist expertise to primary and secondary healthcare, improve productivity and reduce inequalities in access to care.The report says India has already built the foundations for AI in healthcare through initiatives such as the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, IndiaAI Mission, SAHI, BODH and the National Medical Devices Policy, 2023. It says the next challenge is to move AI from successful pilot projects to routine clinical use by creating AI-ready health data, a predictable regulatory framework and reimbursement mechanisms for AI-enabled technologies.
Article Summary: India's healthcare system is coming under growing pressure from an ageing population, rising burden of chronic diseases and shortages of doctors, nurses and hospital beds. The report says artificial intelligence can help bridge this widening gap by extending specialist expertise, improving diagnosis and expanding access to quality healthcare.

NEW DELHI: Meta's platforms must comply with Indian law and cannot be governed solely by the company's global policies, news agency ANI reported quoting government sources said on Sunday.This follows a series of meetings between the social media giant and the ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY). Officials also clarified that it would be factually incorrect to say the government had "directed Meta to completely overhaul its algorithm".The government’s focus, is on ensuring that Meta’s content policies, platform guidelines and moderation systems are aligned with Indian law. While concerns remain, officials said the discussions are aimed at securing concrete changes from the company rather than simply seeking assurances, ANI reported quoting sources.Sources told ANI that India's cultural context is not always fully understood by teams based outside the country. They said Meta needs greater local input, including stronger understanding of Indian languages and cultural nuances, to improve content moderation in India.The latest clarification came after a meeting on Friday between Meta's technical team and MeitY officials, during which the company explained its existing systems for handling harmful content online. Technical discussions between the two sides remain underway, with another round of meetings expected next week, sources said.On child sexual abuse material (CSAM), government sources told ANI that there is zero tolerance and zero compromise.Officials said allowing such material to remain on Meta's platforms would amount to a serious violation of rules. They said the company needs to adopt stronger and more proactive measures, with concrete action expected instead of assurances.The issue was also raised during earlier meetings between Meta's global team and government officials, amid wider concerns over the company's content moderation systems.The government has also raised concerns over deepfakes involving prominent personalities.Sources told ANI that content posted from authorised or verified handles should not be incorrectly identified as deepfakes. Officials said such sensitive cases cannot be left entirely to automated detection systems and called for a "human-in-the-loop" mechanism to ensure content is properly reviewed before any takedown.The users are frequently shown content unrelated to their stated interests and whether this points to shortcomings in Meta's recommendation systems, ANI reported.Officials also asked why synthetically generated content continues to be amplified through the company's algorithms.The government has insisted that once such content is flagged, it should not be recommended further or repeatedly resurface on the platform, sources said.The issue of Meta's recommendation systems had also figured in earlier meetings with IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and senior ministry officials, when the company's global team was questioned about its algorithms and compliance with Indian laws.The latest discussions follow several rounds of engagement between Meta and the Indian government over deepfakes, CSAM, bot accounts, synthetic content and the company's compliance with Indian laws.According to earlier reports, Meta's technical team had explained its proposed measures to address the concerns raised by the government and said it had solutions to tackle deepfakes, CSAM and bot accounts.The government has also been examining Meta's compliance with intermediary provisions under Indian law, including the Article Title: Government spending on education below Unesco's 15% standard
Article Text:
The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India remains just above Unesco's minimum GDP benchmark for education, but the sector's share in government spending has slipped below the prescribed threshold. Education accounts for 4.1% of GDP but 14.2% of total public expenditure, down from 15.7% in 2015 and below the 15% benchmark, Unesco's 2026 SDG 4 scorecard has shown.The funding picture assumes significance because India continues to lag on secondary school completion. Its latest lower secondary (Classes VI-VIII) completion rate is 86% as against its 99% national benchmark for 2025, while upper secondary (Classes IX-XII) completion rate is 51% as against 84%. Unesco classifies progress at both levels as slow.Under the Education 2030 framework, countries committed to spending 4-6% of GDP and/or 15-20% of public expenditure on education. The scorecard uses the lower thresholds as minimum benchmarks. India meets one. Its spending on education has remained at 4.1% of GDP since 2015, but its share of public expenditure has declined 1.5 percentage points to 14.2%.Among major emerging economies, China too meets one benchmark, at 4% of GDP (11.9% of public spending), while figures for Brazil are 5.6% and 12.9%. South Africa meets both, at 6% and 19.1%, while Indonesia, Bangladesh and Pakistan meet neither.The pattern is common among developed economies too: the US, UK, Germany and France meet the GDP threshold but not the public expenditure benchmark, while Sweden and Switzerland meet both.Unesco noted that richer countries tend to meet the GDP benchmark but not the public expenditure threshold because they raise more revenue, while education often accounts for a larger share of budgets in poorer countries.Latest data show 39 of 205 countries, or 19%, meeting both benchmarks, while 72, or 35%, meet neither. Another 64 countries, including India, spend above 4% of GDP but below 15% of public expenditure. Among high-income countries, 11% meet both benchmarks and 50% follow India's pattern.India, however, has larger unmet schooling needs. Lower secondary completion has risen from 81% in 2015 to 86% but remains 13 percentage points below its 99% benchmark. Even Unesco's "feasible" 2025 benchmark of 90% is four points above the latest rate.This is despite programmes operating at scale. Unesco's India profile says Samagra Shiksha supports about 15.6 crore learners, while PM-Poshan covers around 11.8 crore children in 11.2 lakh government and aided schools. The trend is part of a broader global concern. The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.
Article Summary: Education accounts for 4.1% of GDP but 14.2% of total public expenditure. This is down from 15.7% in 2015 and below the 15% benchmark, Unesco says. The funding picture assumes significance because India continues to lag on secondary school completion.

In a major crackdown on regulatory fraud in the pharmaceutical sector, the Centre has amended the Drugs Rules, 1945 to empower drug regulators to temporarily debar companies that submit fake or fabricated data while seeking approvals for drugs and related licences.Under the amended rules notified by the Union health ministry on Thursday, applicants found submitting fabricated data will not only face rejection of their applications or cancellation of existing licences, but can also be barred from filing fresh applications before the concerned licensing authority, whether at the Centre or in the states, for a specified period. Fabricated data undermines the integrity of the approval process, raises questions about the quality of medicines and can pose serious risks to public health.The amendment is intended to strengthen accountability and ensure that drug approvals are backed by reliable scientific evidence.Officials said the amendment is part of the government's broader effort to align India's drug regulatory framework with global best practices by promoting ethical compliance while taking stricter action against companies that indulge in malpractice.
Article Summary: New provision will apply to all applications filed under Drugs Rules, 1945. Aim is to deter companies from submitting false scientific data to secure regulatory approvals. Amid repeated appeals of the chair to the opposition MPs to go back to their seats before he could call LoP, Rijiju raised a point of order. Citing rules, he said Kharge has been saying the same thing every day, and that is a rule against repetition.When the House reconvened at noon, protests continued. Heeding the opposition's request, the chairperson asked Kharge to speak. But the treasury benches objected to this. Amid protests from both sides, Kharge said, "If I don't read the rules, if I don't read my matter, should I read what you (Rijiju) give? It's my right, what to speak, when to speak, how to speak."Kharge said they have been asking PM and Shah to come to the House. "We request the chair to direct the home minister to come and give a statement...," he said. Rijiju objected that Kharge cannot dictate which minister should come on which date. Responding to this, Radhakrishnan said, "No, he (Kharge) is not dictating. He has put his request... As parliamentary affairs minister, you have to reflect the sentiments to HM..."In a press conference, Kharge said they had been demanding Shah's statement on police "excess" against students for the past 15 days and that the PM should apologise to students, but both have been absent from Parliament. "We requested the RS chair that we want the PM's apology and the HM's statement," he said.
Article Summary: The Appropriation Bill, 2026 authorises withdrawal of funds from the Consolidated Fund of India to cover excess expenditure of around Rs 54,067 crore incurred on certain services. The bill was returned to Lok Sabha after the members' approval through a voice vote - completing the parliamentary process for a Money Bill.
